chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job and the home

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What a home health aide does and how to get trained
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe the home health aide role and list the steps to get trained in your state.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state's official page and an agency's job post, you will describe what a home health aide does and the steps to get trained in your state, naming the training, the test or competency check, and the page you checked.
Home health aides and personal care aides both help people at home with daily tasks like bathing, dressing, meals and laundry. Home health aides may also do basic health tasks, such as checking pulse, temperature and breathing, depending on the state. They are supervised by nurses or other medical staff.
Personal care aides usually give non-medical help, such as companionship, cleaning, cooking and driving. Job posts often use both titles, so read the duties.
Home health and hospice agencies that are paid by Medicare must follow federal rules about their aides. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics says aides at these agencies must finish formal training and pass a standardized test. Some states also require a license or certification, a background check or a competency exam.
This course prepares you. Your training and test come from an agency or approved program. To check your state's rules, go to your state's board or department of health. Many agencies train new aides, sometimes for free, so ask.
Step by step:
- Search for your state's name plus "home health aide training requirements" and open the state health department page.
- Write down the training, test and background check rules.
- Look at two job posts from home health agencies near you and list the duties and requirements.
- Ask each agency whether it trains new aides.
Words to know:
- Home health aide (HHA): a trained aide who gives personal care and some basic health tasks in a client's home, supervised by a nurse.
- Personal care aide: an aide who gives non-medical help at home, like cleaning, cooking and companionship.
- Agency: a company that sends aides and nurses to clients' homes.
- Competency test: a test that checks you know and can do the job's skills.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Home Health and Personal Care Aides
- CareerOneStop: Find an American Job Center
Try it now: Find your state's official page on home health aide rules. Then find one home health agency job post near you. On paper, write the training rule from the state page, three duties from the job post, and one question you would ask the agency.
You can now explain what a home health aide does and find your state's training rules on an official page.

check.q: Who supervises a home health aide?
options: A nurse or other medical staff
check.why: Home health aides are supervised by nurses or other medical staff.

check.q: Where do you check training rules for home health aides in your state?
options: Your state's board or department of health
check.why: The state's official health page sets and explains the rules.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Checking a client's home for safety
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the safety hazards in a home and what to do about each.
This lesson builds toward: Given a picture or description of a client's home, you will list the safety hazards and what you would do about each, finding at least 4 hazards, including one for your own safety.
A home is not a hospital. Every home is different, so look around each time you arrive. Falls are one of the biggest dangers for older adults. MedlinePlus lists ways to lower the risk: remove tripping hazards, have rails on stairs and in the tub or shower, and keep eyes checked.
Look for loose rugs, cords across the floor, clutter on stairs, poor lighting, a wet bathroom floor and things the client must reach up high for. Tell your supervisor about hazards you cannot fix, and never move furniture or throw things away without asking the client.
Germs matter at home too. Clean your hands before and after care, wear gloves when you may touch body fluids, and clean your hands right after you take gloves off. Use soap and water when your hands look dirty.
Keep yourself safe. Know the address and your agency's phone number. Ask that pets be put away if they make you uneasy. If you ever feel unsafe, leave and call your supervisor. You are not expected to stay in danger.
Step by step:
- Look around as you arrive: floors, stairs, lighting, bathroom.
- Fix small hazards with the client's OK, like a cord across the path.
- Write down and report hazards you cannot fix.
- If you feel unsafe, leave and call your supervisor.
Words to know:
- Hazard: something that could cause an injury, like a loose rug.
- Fall risk: how likely a person is to fall.
- Grab bar: a strong bar fixed to the wall to hold on to, often by the toilet or tub.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Falls
- CDC: Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
Try it now: Walk through your own home as if you were a home health aide. List at least four hazards you find (for example a loose rug or a dark hallway), what you would do about each, and one thing you would do to stay safe yourself.
You can now check a home for hazards, fix or report them, and protect your own safety on a visit.

check.q: You see a lamp cord across the path to the bathroom. What do you do?
options: With the client's OK, move it out of the path
check.why: Moving a tripping hazard with the client's OK lowers the fall risk.

check.q: A visitor at the client's home makes threats and you feel unsafe. What do you do?
options: Stay and finish all tasks first
check.why: Your safety comes first; leave and call your supervisor.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Following the care plan with dignity
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put a visit's care-plan tasks in order and do them in a way that respects the client.
This lesson builds toward: Given a care plan for a made-up client, you will put the visit tasks in order and do each in a way that protects the client's dignity and choices, staying inside the care plan.
The nurse writes a care plan for each client. It says what you do on each visit: for example help with a shower, help getting dressed, make lunch, a short walk, and laundry. Do what the plan says. If the client asks for something that is not on the plan, call your supervisor.
Aides do not change the care plan and do not give medical advice. Depending on the state and the plan, you may remind a client that it is time for their medicine, but you do not decide doses or change medicines. Questions about medicines go to the nurse.
Dignity means treating the client as an adult in charge of their own life. Knock, greet them by the name they prefer, explain what you will do and ask before you start. Offer choices, like which shirt to wear. Let them do what they can for themselves, even if it takes longer. Keep them covered during bathing.
Hands-on tasks such as transfers and bathing someone who cannot stand are learned and checked in your training, under a nurse's supervision.
Step by step:
- Read the care plan before you start.
- Greet the client, explain the plan for today and ask about their wishes.
- Do the tasks in a sensible order, for example bathe before dressing, and meals on time.
- Let the client do what they can and offer choices.
- Call your supervisor about anything not on the plan.
Words to know:
- Care plan: the nurse's written list of what care the client gets and how.
- Dignity: treating a person with respect, as an adult who makes their own choices.
- Scope: the tasks you are trained and allowed to do in your job.
Try it now: Practice only, made-up client: Mrs. Okafor's care plan says "laundry, help with shower, help with dressing, lunch at noon, 10-minute walk after lunch". You arrive at 10:30. Write the tasks in the order you would do them and one way you would offer her a choice in each.
You can now follow a care plan in a sensible order, stay inside your role and respect the client's dignity and choices.

check.q: A client asks you to clean their gutters, which is not on the care plan. What do you do?
options: Call your supervisor about the request
Ask a friend to do it for money
check.why: Tasks not on the care plan go to your supervisor.

check.q: A client wants to button their own shirt but is slow. What do you do?
options: Do it for them to save time
Let them do it and help only if they ask
check.why: Letting clients do what they can protects their dignity and independence.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Reporting, privacy and your visit kit

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Watching for changes and writing a visit note
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a factual visit note and choose whether to call the nurse or 911.
This lesson builds toward: Given a change you notice on a visit, you will write a factual visit note and choose whether to call the nurse or 911, with the time, what you saw or heard, and who you told.
You may be the only person who sees the client today. Watch for changes: eating or drinking less, new pain, a new sore or bruise, more confusion, trouble breathing, a fall, or a change in mood.
Write your visit note with facts: what you did, what you saw and heard, and the time. Use the client's own words in quotes. "11:00. Helped with shower. Red area on right heel, size of a coin. Client said, 'My heel hurts.'" is a good note. "Seemed off" is not.
Call your supervisor or nurse about any change. Call 911 first for an emergency: trouble breathing, chest pain, a person who will not wake up, heavy bleeding, or signs of a stroke. Then call your agency.
Your agency will tell you how it wants notes written, on paper or in an app. Never write private details anywhere else, like your own phone's notes.
Step by step:
- Notice the change.
- Emergency? Call 911 first, then your agency.
- Not an emergency? Call your nurse or supervisor.
- Write the facts, the time, the client's words and who you told.
Words to know:
- Visit note: the record an aide writes about each visit.
- Emergency: a sudden, serious danger to life or health that needs 911.
- Pressure sore: damaged skin from staying in one position too long; often starts as a red area over a bone.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Pressure Sores
Try it now: Practice only, made-up client: "Mr. Diaz usually eats all his lunch. Today he ate two bites, said 'I don't feel like eating,' and his left ankle looks more swollen than last week." Write a three-line visit note and decide: call the nurse, or call 911? Write why.
You can now write a factual visit note and choose whether a change needs the nurse or 911.

check.q: Your client has sudden trouble breathing. What do you do first?
options: Wait to see if it passes
check.why: Trouble breathing is an emergency; call 911 first, then the agency.

options: "1:15. Ate 2 bites of lunch. Said, 'I'm not hungry.'"
check.why: It gives the time, what was measured and the client's words.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Privacy, money and boundaries
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the action that protects a client's privacy, money and safety.
This lesson builds toward: Given a situation about privacy, money, gifts or possible abuse, you will choose the action that protects the client and follows the rules, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
A client's health information is private. HIPAA, a federal law, protects it. Share it only with your care team. Do not talk about clients with friends, post about them or take photos in their home.
Keep clear boundaries about money and gifts. Never borrow money, lend money, take gifts of value or use a client's card unless your agency's rules and the care plan allow a task like shopping with receipts. Follow your agency's rules exactly, and keep receipts.
Older and disabled adults can be victims of abuse, neglect and money theft, sometimes by people close to them. Warning signs include bruises nobody can explain, poor hygiene, bed sores, fear or withdrawal, and sudden changes with money.
If you suspect abuse, tell your supervisor right away. You can also contact Adult Protective Services in your state. If the client is in danger now, call 911. Some states require aides to report; your agency will tell you how.
Step by step:
- Share client information only with the care team.
- Follow agency rules about money, keep receipts, and refuse gifts of value.
- Watch for signs of abuse, neglect or money theft.
- Report concerns to your supervisor, or Adult Protective Services; call 911 for danger.
Words to know:
- HIPAA: a federal law that protects the privacy of health information.
- Boundary: a clear limit on what you do in a work relationship.
- Financial exploitation: taking or misusing someone's money or belongings.
- Adult Protective Services (APS): the state or county office that looks into abuse and neglect of older or disabled adults.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Elder Abuse
- Eldercare Locator (ACL)
Try it now: Read these three made-up situations and write what you would do: 1) The client offers you $200 "for being so kind." 2) The client's nephew asks for the client's bank card PIN. 3) Your friend asks which famous person you care for. Then write one boundary sentence you could say kindly.
You can now protect a client's privacy, money and safety and report concerns to the right person.

check.q: A client offers you an expensive watch as a thank-you. What do you do?
options: Kindly say no and tell your supervisor
Sell it and split the money
check.why: Gifts of value cross a boundary; refuse kindly and follow agency rules.

check.q: You notice the client's money keeps disappearing after a relative visits. What do you do?
options: Ignore it, it is family business
Hide the client's wallet in your bag
check.why: Possible financial exploitation is reported to your supervisor or Adult Protective Services.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your practice visit kit and next steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a practice visit kit for a made-up client and plan your next step toward training.
This lesson builds toward: Given a picture or description of a client's home, you will list the safety hazards and what you would do about each, finding at least 4 hazards, including one for your own safety. Given a care plan for a made-up client, you will put the visit tasks in order and do each in a way that protects the client's dignity and choices, staying inside the care plan. Given a change you notice on a visit, you will write a factual visit note and choose whether to call the nurse or 911, with the time, what you saw or heard, and who you told. Using your state's official page and an agency's job post, you will describe what a home health aide does and the steps to get trained in your state, naming the training, the test or competency check, and the page you checked.
Now you will put the course together. A visit kit is what a prepared aide carries in their head and on paper: a quick home safety check, the care-plan tasks in order, and a clear visit note.
Use a made-up client, for example "Mr. Johnson, 78, lives alone, uses a walker, care plan: help with shower, dress, make breakfast, short walk, laundry." Never use a real person's name or details for practice.
Then take one real step toward the job. Find a home health agency or approved program near you that trains new aides. Ask about training, the test, the background check, pay during training and the schedule. An American Job Center can help you find and pay for training.
On a résumé, list caregiving you have done, such as caring for a family member, in plain words: "Helped a family member with meals, bathing and appointments for 2 years."
Step by step:
- Write a home safety checklist with at least 6 items.
- List the made-up client's care-plan tasks in the order you would do them.
- Write a factual visit note with one change you would report, and who you would tell.
- Write your state's official page and one agency or program you will contact this week.
Words to know:
- Visit kit: your checklist, task list and note format for each visit.
- Approved program: a training program your state or a certified agency accepts.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Home Health and Personal Care Aides (How to Become One)
Try it now: Final task: make your practice visit kit for a made-up client: a home safety checklist, the care-plan tasks in order, a factual visit note with one change you would report and to whom, and your state's official page plus one agency or program you will contact.
You can now put together a practice visit kit and take a real next step toward home health aide training.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Home safety checklist Fewer than 4 items, or no item for the aide's own safety. At least 6 items covering floors, stairs, lighting, bathroom, germs and the aide's safety. Says what to do about each item: fix with the client's OK, or report. Care-plan tasks Tasks are missing, out of a sensible order, or outside the plan. All plan tasks in a sensible order, with one way to offer a choice. Notes which tasks the client can do part of themselves. Visit note The note has guesses or opinions, or no time. Facts, the time, the client's own words and who was told. Correctly says whether the change needs the nurse or 911, and why. Privacy kept The kit uses a real person's name or private details. Uses a made-up client and no private details. Adds one boundary sentence about money or gifts. Next step No official page or agency listed. Lists the state's official page and one agency or program to contact. Lists the questions to ask about training, test, background check and pay. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: What is a good question to ask a home health agency?
options: "Do you train new aides, and is there a test?"
"Can I give medicines my own way?"
"Can I bring my friends to clients' homes?"
check.why: Asking about training and testing tells you the real path at that agency.

check.q: Your made-up care plan says shower, dress and breakfast. Which order makes sense?
check.why: Bathing before dressing, then a meal, is a sensible order for these tasks.
